Decision: Can one project hold multiple active client contracts?
CurrentEvidence: Today impossible: contract terms are columns on Project (Models/Context/Accounting/Dimensions.cs:36-44), so exactly one implicit contract exists.
Options: (a) one contract per project; (b) many contracts per project with scope split; (c) one contract spanning many projects (programme)
Recommendation: (b) — a separate ClientContract entity with a project link, because packages and phased awards are normal in contracting and (a) forces fake projects.
Consequences: (b) means BOQ, certificates and retention all key on ContractId, not ProjectId — a wider change in C3.
BlockingScope: Blocks C3 and the certificate design

Decision: Do the client BOQ and the internal cost estimate share one structure?
CurrentEvidence: Today one structure: BoqItem holds the client UnitPrice AND four estimated cost buckets on the same row (Boq.cs:20-25).
Options: (a) keep one row with both; (b) separate client BOQ from internal estimate, linked
Recommendation: (b) — the client BOQ is contractual and immutable once approved, the internal estimate changes constantly; sharing a row is what makes rate changes dangerous.
Consequences: (b) requires a migration path for existing BoqItem cost buckets and a mapping UI.

Decision: What are the certification approval limits?
CurrentEvidence: None exist: ApproveAsync only checks Draft and GrossWork>0 (BL/ProgressBillingService.cs:191-200).
Options: (a) single approver; (b) value-banded approvers; (c) role chain regardless of value
Recommendation: (b) with a role chain floor — value bands are how contracting firms actually delegate.
Consequences: Needs a limits table and the approval engine of CR-14.

CurrentEvidence: Flat percent of period work: R = W x Project.RetentionPercent (BL/ProgressBillingService.cs:118).
Options: (a) flat percent per certificate; (b) percent capped at a contract ceiling; (c) tiered (higher until X% complete, then lower); (d) per-BOQ-item applicability
Recommendation: (b)+(d) — a ceiling and an item-level applicability flag cover most Gulf contracts; (c) as an optional method.
Consequences: Changes the certificate computation and needs a retention term set on the contract.

CurrentEvidence: Pro-rata per certificate, capped at the remaining 2104 balance (BL/ProgressBillingService.cs:120).
Options: (a) pro-rata (today); (b) start after X% progress; (c) fixed instalments; (d) back-loaded
Recommendation: Keep (a) as default, add (b) as a contract term — (b) is common and today unrepresentable.
Consequences: Advance recovery rules move onto the contract entity.

Decision: How are materials on site (MOS) valued in a certificate?
CurrentEvidence: Not supported: the certificate has no MOS concept (Models/Context/Accounting/ProgressBilling.cs).
Options: (a) not certified at all; (b) at invoice cost; (c) at BOQ material rate; (d) at a contractual percentage of value
Recommendation: (d) with (b) as the valuation base — the contract usually caps MOS at a percentage.
Consequences: Introduces a non-work component in the certificate that must be recovered as the work is executed.

Decision: What is the subcontractor over-certification policy?
Options: (a) hard block at allocated scope; (b) allow with an approved variation; (c) allow with a warning
Recommendation: (a) as the default with (b) as the authorised exception. (c) is what effectively happens today and it is the defect.
Consequences: Requires SubcontractScope in C3 before any subcontractor certificate work in C6.

Decision: Does budget overspend block or warn?
CurrentEvidence: Neither: there is no budget entity and no commitment check anywhere (BL/ProjectBudgetService.cs is a report).
Options: (a) warn only; (b) block at approval of PO/subcontract; (c) per-company policy switch
Recommendation: (c) defaulting to warn — blocking procurement is a business risk the owner must choose, not us.
Consequences: A blocking mode reaches into Purchasing approval, which is another module's behaviour.

Decision: What are the cost transfer rules between cost codes?
CurrentEvidence: No cost codes and no transfer exist.
Options: (a) no transfers; (b) transfers with approval and reason; (c) free transfer inside a category
Recommendation: (b) — a transfer is a commercial decision and must leave a reason and an approver.

Decision: May one site access another site's warehouse?
CurrentEvidence: Unconstrained: a warehouse has no site and no project (Models/Context/Inventory/Inventory.cs:144-159); any warehouse can be picked on a project material issue.
Options: (a) site-restricted; (b) restricted with an approved exception; (c) unrestricted
Recommendation: (b) — cross-site borrowing is real but must be visible.
Consequences: Requires Warehouse.SiteId (an Inventory-owned change) or a construction-side site-warehouse map.

Decision: What is the drawing approval workflow?
Options: (a) issue-only register; (b) internal review then issue; (c) consultant approval cycle with status codes (A/B/C)
Recommendation: (c) — consultant status codes are the norm and drive whether the site may build.
Consequences: Determines whether a superseded revision is blocked or warned (screen 26).

Decision: What is the mobile offline policy?
CurrentEvidence: No mobile construction surface exists yet (crossbuy_mobile/lib/screens/ has no project screen).
Options: (a) online only; (b) offline draft, server authoritative; (c) full offline with conflict merge
Recommendation: (b) — drafts offline, every posting online, idempotency key per document. (c) is where duplicated site data comes from.
Consequences: Sets the CR-18 contract before any mobile build.

Decision: What are the project closeout rules?
CurrentEvidence: A Close permission exists with no process (BL/ProjectsAccessService.cs:41).
Options: (a) status change only; (b) checklist-gated close that locks cost and certificates; (c) close plus a separate DLP-active state
Recommendation: (c) — a closed project with an active DLP is the real end state, and retention is still outstanding.
Consequences: Needs handover, DLP and a lock on new cost/certificates.
